passage: In the school hostel study hall, Akash sat with his phone, thinking about a lazy evening. Then he remembered: seven o'clock, call with Usha. Yesterday they had agreed that both would be on a call, cameras off, each would say a target, and then they would work for forty minutes. "If I'm late, Usha waits, and I'll feel bad," he whispered to himself. He opened the physics book at five to seven. At seven Usha's voice came: "Ready? I'm doing two history chapters." "Numericals from chapter six," said Akash. They went quiet. When the call ended, he had done nine problems, on an evening he would normally have spent on videos. "Same time tomorrow," said Usha.

qa.q: What did Akash plan to work on during the call?
qa.a: Akash planned numericals from chapter six.

qa.q: How was Akash feeling as he considered a lazy evening?
qa.a: Akash was tempted by a lazy evening, but felt it would be unfair to keep Usha waiting, and that guilt pushed him to start.

qa.q: What could Akash and Usha add to keep the habit going?
qa.a: They could share one line about what they finished at the end of each call, or agree what to do if one cannot join.

qa.q: How might Usha feel about Akash arriving on time?
qa.a: Usha may feel supported and encouraged, since each of them starting on time helps both.

grounding: Shows a teenager pairing with a classmate for evening study calls and starting on time because someone is waiting.

subtype: Approach: studies with a friend who has a similar goal [Thinking]
passage:
Dear Shreya Didi,

You asked how my studying is going this term. Honestly, better than ever, and it's because of one small thing. My classmate Harman and I both want to improve in physics, so we started a video call every evening at 7:30. We don't even talk much. We just keep our cameras on and do our own problems.

What I've noticed is this: when I'm alone, I say "five more minutes" till nine. But if I know Harman is sitting there waiting at 7:30, I'd feel embarrassed to join late. So I'm at my desk by 7:30, even on days I'm feeling lazy. Last week I had a cold and still sat down at 7:30.

Physics marks up from 52 to 68.

Your brother,
Baljeet

qa.q: At what time do Baljeet and Harman start their call?
Why does Baljeet start on time, even on lazy days?
qa.a: Baljeet would feel embarrassed to keep Harman waiting, so the thought of someone at 7:30 beats the urge to delay.

qa.q: What else could Baljeet try on nights when Harman can't join?
qa.a: Keep the same 7:30 start and message Harman a photo of the finished problems, so the habit holds.

qa.q: How might Harman be affected by these calls?
qa.a: Harman probably benefits the same way, starting on time because Baljeet is waiting too.

grounding: A teenager pairs with a classmate for evening study calls, and knowing someone is waiting makes Baljeet start on time.

subtype: Approach: studies with a friend who has a similar goal [Thinking]
passage: So, I'm Yash, and my study problem was simple: I'd sit down "at seven" and actually start at nine. My friend Vidya had the same problem with maths. One day she said, "What if we call each other at seven and just study with the call on?" I thought it was silly. But here's what I worked out after a week. When it's just me, nobody knows I'm late. When Vidya's face is already on the screen at seven, with her book open, I can't make her wait. It would feel rude. So I'm at my desk at 6:58 now. On the days I feel lazy, it's even more useful, because that's exactly when I'd have skipped.

qa.q: What time does Yash sit at the desk now?
How would Yash feel making Vidya wait?
qa.a: Yash would feel rude and a little guilty, which is why starting late no longer happens.

qa.q: What could Yash and Vidya try if the calls start turning into chatting?
qa.a: Agree to talk only for five minutes at the start, then study silently with cameras on.

qa.q: How might Vidya see the arrangement?
qa.a: Vidya, whose idea it was, probably feels pleased it works for both of them and that she has a steady partner.

grounding: A teenager realises that knowing a study partner is waiting means starting on time, even on lazy days.
